newsitem.title: INDONESIA: More sporadic violence seen before Indonesia poll.
newsitem.headline: More sporadic violence seen before Indonesia poll.

text.p: The official start of campaigning for Indonesia's May 29 general elections is two weeks away, but political tensions are already running high and scattered violence may recur, analysts said on Monday.

Riots have broken out in four towns in Central Java province in the past two weeks after clashes between supporters of the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) and the ruling Golkar and although the situation is now generally peaceful, tension prevails, they said.
"There is potential for an eruption at any time," said political analyst Arief Budiman. "There could be some scattered conflicts during the campaign."

Budiman, a resident of Salatiga town in Central Java, told Reuters in a telephone interview that rival political parties were staking out their turf ahead of the official start of the campaign on April 27, which was leading to disquiet.

A Golkar campaign to plaster the province with flags carrying its yellow colour has taken shape, but in one area Budiman said he had seen PPP supporters taking them down and replacing them with their own green flags.

A Reuters Television reporter in Central Java at the weekend saw scores of yellow and green flags flying in violation of electoral rules. Trunks of trees along the highway were painted yellow and in one town, a man hanging a banner advertising a retail chain said government officials had insisted the background be yellow.

"The yellowisation campaign has created quite some tension," said a Western diplomat in Jakarta. "It's significant that we're not even into the campaign yet and the situation is already relatively tense. It's put people on edge."
Only three political parties -- the PPP, Golkar and the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) -- are allowed to contest Indonesia's general elections.

With Indonesia's tightly controlled electoral system, Golkar is almost assured of achieving a landslide victory. But analysts have said the current tensions can be traced to its all-out efforts to meet a target of garnering more than 70 percent of the vote, up from around 68 percent at the last poll in 1992.
The PPP won 17 percent and the PDI 15 percent in 1992.

Budiman said the military was reluctant to intervene in the clashes over the last two weeks because they were relatively minor and any action could provoke a backlash. But he said any major flare-up would invite quick army action.
Armed forces commander General Feisal Tanjung said last month the military would deal harshly with anyone who attempted to disrupt the political process.
The military has its eye on Central Java with the army commander for the province, Major General Soebagyo, saying last week that the region was violence-prone.

The official Antara news agency quoted Soebagyo as saying that the province's demographic characteristics made it prone to tensions. He did not elaborate, but the comments were believed to refer to the high population density in Central Java and the sharp political polarisation among its people.
Indonesia's financial markets were also prepared for some violence ahead of the elections although analysts were generally taking a benign view.
"Any disturbances during the election season, and there are likely to be some, should be viewed as a buying opportunity," said a report by Peregrine Securities brokerage this week.

"Outbreaks of riots could pick up in the lead-up to the May general election, and although this has done little to rock the market, investors are likely to react differently if any riots take place in the capital," said Jos Parengkuan of Lippo Securities.
